Andrews), Herp Update: Gray Treefrogs are freeze tolerant; water between their cells freezes, heart and lungs stop, cell sugars act as antifreeze; they thaw out in spring perfectly healthy without having eaten in seven months; probably overwinter in leaf litter; https://www.vtherpatlas.org/?p=4339

The Canadian Encyclopedia, Gray Treefrog: can survive having more than 40 per cent of its body fluids freeze without ill effect, protecting cells with glucose and glycerol; overwinters under leaf litter and snow; can change colour rapidly; large toepads for climbing; up to 6 cm; its trill is one of the loudest frog calls in North America; females lay up to 2,600 eggs a year; undersides of thighs bright yellow-orange, usually hidden; cannot be told apart by sight from Cope's gray treefrog; https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/gray-treefrog

University of Georgia, Savannah River Ecology Lab Herpetology, Cope's Gray Treefrog: skin secretions contain toxins that may irritate eyes, lips, mucous membranes and open cuts, wash hands after handling; colour mottled gray to light green, shifts with surroundings; bright yellow-orange flash colours on the inner thighs; D. chrysoscelis is diploid and D. versicolor tetraploid, morphologically indistinguishable; https://srelherp.uga.edu/frogs-and-toads/copes-gray-treefrog/

beats.say: This frog freezes every winter. Its heart stops. And in spring, it hops away.
The gray tree frog. Smaller than your palm, with big sticky toe pads.
In fall, it hides under dead leaves and snow.
Then the ice comes. The water between its cells turns to ice.
Inside, sugars work like antifreeze, and keep each cell from freezing.
Its heart stops. Its lungs stop. And it just... waits.
More than forty percent of the fluid in its body can freeze, and it's fine.
Then spring comes. It thaws out, perfectly healthy, after seven months without a meal.
It climbs straight up tree bark with those toes.
Its thighs hide a secret. Bright yellow orange, flashed when it stretches its legs.
And its call is one of the loudest of any frog in North America.
A female can lay up to twenty six hundred eggs in one year.
It has a twin species. They look exactly the same.
But one of them has twice as many chromosomes.
Careful. Its skin has toxins that can irritate your eyes and lips. Wash your hands after.
Would you pick up a frozen frog?
No heartbeat all winter, and it still gets up before you do.
Follow me. Next, an animal with a heart two feet long.
